correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the section integration: the reflected-simplex coefficients are binomial(n,k)^2 and the beta integral reduces their weighted sum to (n+1)^(n-1). For the shifted polar the fiber above u has positive length (2−(1−z)max t_i+(1+z)n min t_i)/(1−z²), t_i=<u,v_i>. The Gram determinant of the difference matrix on the zero-sum hyperplane is n+1, and the regular-simplex length scale is sqrt((n+1)/n); the ordered gap integral therefore gives the Euclidean prefactor and the stated a_{n,k}. The log-product derivative is strictly increasing, negative at zero and divergent at one. With δ=1−z, write a_{n,k}=2nk(1−δ b_{n,k}), b_{n,k}=(n+1)(k−1)/(2nk). Their sum is (n+1)(n−H_n)/(2n); the stationary equation gives δ=2/n+O(log n/n²), and the inverse correction product tends to e. The remaining prefactor gives e² n^n/(n!)², while the simplex benchmark is asymptotic to e² n^n/(n!)² before multiplying by the correction e. The n=2 radical and product agree by substitution and separate high-precision arithmetic. At z=0 the polar constraints are (s−1)/n≤t_i≤1+s, with ∑t_i=0. They force −1≤s≤1 and the bounds are always distinct; each choice of one bound per i gives a unique feasible vertex. Subsets of these compatible choices are exactly the face incidences, giving the cube. Changing to any interior polarity center preserves this lattice. The optimized product in the claim is for the Cayley body, not a separate minimization over centers of its polar. Inspected VERIFICATION.md and verify_cayley.py; the 35 reported numerical comparisons are supporting finite checks, not an all-dimensional proof or a fresh run.

The latter's Finding (2) gives a beta-product formula for the primal ratio-bounded region. In t coordinates the axial polar projection has A max t−B min t≤2, with A=1−z, B=(1+z)n. For B>A, setting x_i=(t_i+2/(B−A))/(2(n+1)/(B−A)) puts that projection in sum-one coordinates with x_i≤(B/A)x_j. For A>B reflect t, and at equality take the continuous limit.
